summary: The Earth Information Jukebox is a web app that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live sound, built for blind and low-vision people first. It plays three NASA Scientific Visualization Studio datasets on a spinnable 3D globe: ocean temperature, lightning seen from the International Space Station, and aerosols. Every sound comes from the data on the side of the planet facing you: warmer water plays higher notes, busier storms play busier drums, and dust, smoke, sea salt and sulfates each have their own instrument. New listeners can start with a narrated, fully captioned guided show that flies around the planet and teaches each sound on its own (for example, a single tone climbing in pitch as the camera sweeps from the icy North Pole to the warm equator), then hands over the globe. From there, point anywhere to hear that spot, steer with the keyboard, or have values read aloud. Behind the music, a pipeline turns each visualization's colors back into real data values, so what you hear is what NASA's data shows. Earth science is usually only seen; this lets anyone hear it, and gives sighted users a second way to notice patterns in our changing planet.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The site opens on a cinematic globe. "Start the show" begins a narrated, captioned tour (about 2 minutes 20 seconds) that introduces each sound on its own, then hands over the planet. "Explore on my own" goes straight to the globe. Three NASA datasets are on the shelf:

• Ocean temperature (ECCO2, March 2007 to March 2008). A slow chord follows the average sea-surface temperature facing you, and warmer water makes it higher and brighter. A four-note melody plays the globe from left to right, one note per slice. Pointing at a spot plays a single tone whose pitch is the temperature there; in the guided show, that tone climbs almost two and a half octaves as the camera sweeps from 0.1 °C near the North Pole to 27.5 °C at the equator.

• Lightning (ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor, 2017 to 2023). Drums on sixteenth notes whose density and loudness follow new flashes on the visible side. Pitch follows latitude, stereo position follows longitude, thunder accents mark big bursts, and a low drone swells with global storm activity. The flashes are drawn as 1.86 million real dots over NASA's Black Marble city-lights map.

• Aerosols (GEOS-FP, August to September 2024). Four voices: smoke crackles, dust is a low drone, sea salt is an airy shimmer, and sulfates are bell tones. Each grows louder with how much of its particle is in view, and pans left or right with it.

A large readout names what is under the cursor or at the center of the view ("27.6 °C", "Scattered flashes", "Dust" with bars for the four aerosol types).

ACCESSIBILITY (THE CENTRAL GOAL)

• Everything works from the keyboard: arrow keys spin the globe, + and − zoom, and the center of the view plays as it turns.

• Holding Shift reads the value aloud.

• Screen readers get live announcements and labeled controls.

• The guided show has captions for every line, and the data sounds dip while the narrator speaks.

• Reduced-motion settings replace animated transitions.

HOW IT WORKS

• Offline pipeline (Python). It downloads NASA SVS frames and movies, then turns each visualization's colors back into data values using its published colorbar:

– Ocean: temperature in °C.

– Lightning: every flash dot NASA drew, checked against NASA's own frames (we light 87% of NASA's lit pixels).

– Aerosols: each pixel split into the four types by non-negative least squares against the colorbar swatches.

• Web app (JavaScript). three.js renders the globe with NASA's video or stills as its texture. Tone.js synthesizes every sound live in the browser; no data sounds are pre-recorded. Ten times a second, the app measures what is in view and updates the music.

• Loading. Videos start small and upgrade only when the connection can carry them, so the site works on ordinary laptops and school networks.

• Sky. The Sun, Moon, planets and NASA's star map sit behind the Earth at their real positions for each date.

WHY IT'S CREATIVE

The jukebox doesn't attach a soundtrack to a picture: it reads the picture back into data and composes from it. Each dataset gets its own musical character (chords and melody for slow ocean change, percussion for bursty storms, textures for drifting particles), so the three are easy to tell apart by ear, and they still sound musical rather than like beeps.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

• Scientific honesty: every narrated claim was checked against the data at that place and date, and the README states the caveats (for example, lightning dates are approximate).

• Listeners who can't see the screen: sounds are taught one at a time, and every value can be heard or read aloud.

• Judges and students on ordinary hardware and networks: bandwidth-aware video quality and no installs.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Blind and low-vision learners can explore the same NASA Earth data as everyone else, and sighted users get a second way to notice patterns. Next, we want to cover more of the Earth Information Center's catalog, take it into classrooms, museums and planetariums, and test the sounds with blind and low-vision users.

TOOLS

Python, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow and ffmpeg (pipeline); JavaScript, Vite, three.js, Tone.js and WebGL shaders (site); GitHub Pages (hosting). An AI coding assistant helped write and debug the code. The narration voices are AI-generated text-to-speech, and the README and the video say so.

Source code: https://github.com/Brian23443/earth-information-jukebox
